---
title: "Setting up, if you want to drive it"
---

Everything in this book can be read without installing anything. This appendix is for the other
case: running the tool yourself, on the same study, and seeing the numbers appear rather than
taking them on trust.

## What this is

One command builds the environment. It fetches the framework's source at the commit this book
describes, creates an isolated Python environment, fetches the study's data, and then proves the
result by running a check rather than announcing success.

Two of its steps reach outside the clone, and you should know that before running it. The
study's data is cloned as a sparse checkout into a **sibling directory** beside the repository,
named `torivumab-nsclc-301` — about 10 MB of an 81 MB repository. And the clone's own git
configuration is pointed at the repository's hooks, so the consistency checks run on every
commit. `--check` shows what either step would do without doing it.

You need: **git**, **a Python 3.10 or newer somewhere on the machine**, and a browser. Not R —
the analysis runs in the browser.

## What you do

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Lovemore-Gakava/usdm-acdc-in-practice.git
cd usdm-acdc-in-practice
python tools/bootstrap.py
```

If `python` is not found, use `python3` — on macOS and most Linux systems there is no `python`
at all, and on Windows it is often `py -3`. **Do not assume the name.** The script itself runs
on any Python from 3.9, but it builds the environment with the newest 3.10 or later it can find,
because one of the data-reading dependencies needs it — so 3.10 has to exist, not necessarily
be the one you type. It is safe to re-run, and `--check` reports what is missing without
changing anything.

Then start the application, with the environment's interpreter — its path differs by system:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tools/walkthrough.py serve            # macOS, Linux
.venv\Scripts\python.exe tools/walkthrough.py serve    # Windows
```

and open **http://localhost:8080/ac-dc-app/index.html**. Press Ctrl-C to stop it; it cleans up
after itself.

## What you should see

The bootstrap ends by running an alignment check and printing its result — pass counts, and no
failures or skips. A skip means the study data was not found, which means the check ran on the
documents alone.

In the browser, a study list with **TORIVA-LUNG 301** on it. That card is the study definition
from stage 1, read by the application.

## What to look out for

**After the bootstrap, use the environment's interpreter, not the system one.** Anything that
reads the study's data needs it:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tools/check_alignment.py            # macOS, Linux
.venv\Scripts\python.exe tools/check_alignment.py    # Windows
```

A plain `python3` will fail on the import. The tools tell you which interpreter would have
worked, but it is easier to expect it. This is the single most common way a correctly set-up
copy looks broken, and copying the other system's path is the second: the bootstrap's closing
lines print the right one for the machine it ran on.

**On Windows, the engine may refuse to parse until the submodule's line endings are fixed.**
A clone with `core.autocrlf=true` checks the engine's R source out with CRLF endings and R
reports *unexpected invalid token* at the first execution. Once per clone:

```bash
git -C upstream/analysis-concepts config core.autocrlf false
```

then check the file out again. The pinned commit does not change and the submodule stays
clean. This bites at stage 6, and it is the second most common way a correct copy looks
broken.

**The version you get is pinned, deliberately.** The framework is fetched at one commit, and the
study at another, both recorded. The application you see is the one this book describes, not the
latest — which is the point: the standards and the tooling are both moving, and a book that
described a moving target would be wrong within a release. Every screenshot here names the
commit it was taken at.

**Concept reference links will not resolve** unless you supply a CDISC Library key: one line in
a file named `.cdisc-api-key`, in your home directory or the repository root, or the
`CDISC_API_KEY` environment variable. The home directory is the better place, since it keeps the
key out of the working tree altogether. Without one those links answer 401. Nothing else needs
it.

**To rebuild this book** from source, with its figures re-read from the runs:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tools/check_guide.py --render docs/guide/_build      # .venv\Scripts\python.exe on Windows
cd docs/guide/_build && quarto render
```

That needs [Quarto](https://quarto.org). Rendering from the source directory rather than the
build directory publishes the unresolved placeholders instead of the numbers, which is why the
render step exists at all.
